extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and mathematically literate general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for judging mathematical objects, proofs (including computer-assisted proofs), numerical computations, and mathematical models — covering constructivist vs classical standards, verifiability, reliability, and pragmatic acceptance. Targets both pure- and applied-mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of excluded middle (classical vs constructivist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical mathematics applies the law of the excluded middle (every statement is true or false); constructivists deny its applicability in cases like infinite decimal expansions where no constructive method decides P or not-P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For the statement P: 'there eventually occurs a row of 100 successive zeros in the decimal expansion of √2', the constructivist holds that 'Either P or not-P' is not meaningful unless one can constructively determine which. This implies rethinking many classical existence or dichotomy results (e.g., law of trichotomy) from a constructivist viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive truth requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is accepted as true only when there is a constructive procedure (a recipe) that yields evidence of truth; absent such a construction, a statement may be considered neither true nor false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical truth becomes time-dependent in constructivism: it becomes true when someone determines which case holds. The book illustrates this with definitions of numbers given by finite generation rules tied to yet-unfound finite patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition-by-finite-rule standard for real numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining a real number by a rule that specifies how to compute successive finite prefixes (digits) is acceptable; the number is only what these finite parts give us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definition that generates digits until some event (e.g., first run of 100 zeros) is legitimate even if the event may never occur; this highlights that our knowledge of reals is effectively finite and rule-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of existence theorems to justify computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence/uniqueness theorems justify the applied mathematician's belief that a solution u(t) exists and can be studied numerically, even when exact formulas are unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of existence motivates numerical exploration, but does not provide explicit error bounds or a priori stopping rules for approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical stopping criterion for series summation
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, one stops adding terms to a series (e.g., Taylor series) when further terms leave the sum unchanged within desired displayed precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is guided by common sense rather than a rigorous bound on neglected terms; the practitioner accepts this pragmatic stopping despite lack of formal guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability condition for numerical algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms often have rigorous proofs of correctness only under 'reasonable' or typical assumptions; outside these assumptions, the algorithm may fail (e.g., 'blow up').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must watch for indications of abnormal problems (computations breaking down) and recognize that clever counterexamples could produce reasonable-looking but wrong results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software correctness desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, the software used for computations should have rigorous proofs of correctness (proofs-of-programs), though such proofs are time-consuming and rarely available for large systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because full proofs of large compilers and numerical libraries are impractical, users rely on long-term usage, testing, and incremental error correction as pragmatic substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation via independent reruns
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce risk of software/hardware-induced errors, perform the computation independently: run on different systems and with different programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends doing the computation twice, using two different systems/programs on two different machines to detect implementation-specific faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware-failure awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume hardware is highly reliable but not infallible; treat hardware faults as low-probability events that should be detectable (e.g., by gross misbehavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of numerical results is based on likelihood arguments about hardware reliability, not absolute certainty; detection mechanisms and shutdowns are relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and justification of asymptotic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymptotic methods that increase in accuracy as a parameter grows are permissible and often used even without full rigorous justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two different asymptotic methods agree, that agreement is treated as 'almost conclusive' evidence of correctness, even if neither method has a fully rigorous proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement-of-methods heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: If independent computational or asymptotic methods yield agreeing results, this concordance is strong pragmatic evidence for correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is invoked repeatedly: agreement between different methods is treated as an important nonrigorous validation step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-validation by predictive/explanatory value
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical model (e.g., solution of a differential equation) is judged acceptable by how well it predicts or explains the target physical situation—the physical model—after comparing their objective properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both models (mathematical and physical) are studied as distinct realities; validation can come from lab experiments, natural approximations, or simulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification and neglect-of-small-terms justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplified mathematical models obtained by neglecting small terms are acceptable when one can argue (or sometimes prove) closeness to the original model; otherwise they are used heuristically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes one can prove the simplification is justified; often one proceeds on hope/experience and checks whether results 'look reasonable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional verifiability test for proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A classical standard: a sufficiently patient reader should be able to work through a proof and verify its correctness by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-assisted proofs challenge this test because the computational parts cannot be feasibly checked by hand; printing code and data still leaves risks (e.g., mispunched tapes, transient hardware/software faults).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent computational verification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-based parts of proofs should be verified by independent computer programs and/or independent runs (different software/hardware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appel and Haken's referees used an independent program to check reducibility computations; Swinnerton-Dyer and others argue independent replication is the practical route to confidence, paralleling experimental science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance-via-overwhelming_evidence heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: When computational evidence is overwhelming and errors in irrelevant parts won't affect final outcomes, one may reasonably accept the result while acknowledging residual uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swinnerton-Dyer's view: even with rare possible computational errors, the nature of the search makes it 'almost certain' the results are correct; yet he recommends independent attacks if full rigor is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability-of-error tradeoff in long proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: For long and highly computational proofs, the probability of human error in hand verification may exceed the probability of machine error; thus machine assistance can reduce overall error risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an argument for accepting computational assistance in very long proofs, though it does not eliminate all sources of error (software/hardware remain man-made).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic/insight criterion for judging proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond correctness, mathematicians value proofs that provide insight, elegance, and understanding; proofs that are mere large-case computations may be judged less aesthetically valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges this is a matter of taste and that future generations may value computational proofs differently, but aesthetic criteria influence reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable-set/reducibility method standard
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain combinatorial proofs (e.g., four-color theorem), one seeks an unavoidable set of configurations and shows each is reducible; reducibility proofs may require computation when configurations are numerous/complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift from a few hand-checkable configurations (Kempe) to thousands requiring computer reducibility checks (Appel–Haken) illustrates how method complexity changes verification needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for acceptance of very long collaborative proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs span thousands of pages and many contributors, acceptance rests on mutual confidence in the competence and integrity of contributors and on continued reexamination and patching of local errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No absolute guarantees exist; the community relies on social institutions, repeated scrutiny from different perspectives, and the likelihood that significant missed configurations will eventually be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-institutional trust criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical acceptance can be grounded in trust in the professional community and its institutions rather than solely in individual verification of every step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both long human proofs and computer-assisted results are accepted partly because of confidence in the people, processes, and independent rechecks by other researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalism vs practical-numerical distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between formalism as philosophical reduction to axioms and the informal sense of 'formal' numerical calculations (computations without error estimates); applied mathematicians routinely use such 'formal' methods pragmatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The philosophical formalist may dismiss numerical practice as 'not mathematics,' but practitioners rely on a mix of rigorous and pragmatic methods to obtain usable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reconstruction criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructivist programs (e.g., Bishop) aim to reconceive analysis so that formerly nonconstructive results become constructively meaningful, providing an alternative standard of acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion implies reworking much standard analysis; its acceptance depends on philosophical stance and willingness to abandon some classical methods.
